t: Quickstart: from zero to a sent campaign This is the 10-minute path: install, find leads, write the emails, connect your mailbox, and send it safely. Every sending step is dry-run by default . TL;DR: pip install "openleads[all]" → openleads web → Find people → save them to a list → put the list in a sequence. Or stay in the terminal with openleads run . Just looking? openleads demo opens the dashboard on an invented workspace.

pip install "openleads[all]" # engine + chat TUI + sending niceties openleads --version # → openleads 5.1.1 openleads init # friendly first-run setup (optional) Node user? npx openleads works too (it installs the Python package on first run).

Install with pipx so OpenLeads and its Python dependencies stay in an isolated environment: py -m pip install --user pipx py -m pipx ensurepath Close and reopen PowerShell after ensurepath so the updated PATH takes effect, then install and check the CLI: pipx install "openleads[all]" openleads --version openleads init PowerShell accepts double-quoted search phrases directly. Keep the phrase in one quoted argument; a variable works too: openleads find "marketing agencies in Miami" -n 10 $query = 'marketing agencies in Miami' openleads find $query -n 10 The scheduler uses Windows Task Scheduler

openleads doctor doctor tells you, in plain language, what works and what to fix: DNS-over-HTTPS reachable? (needed for MX/SPF/DMARC checks) SMTP port 25 open? If blocked (most home ISPs), don't worry: the engine compensates with Gravatar + ground-truth + learned patterns. OpenRouter key set? Optional; unlocks AI drafting + smarter NL parsing. Mailbox configured + logs in? Needed only for sending . Your sending domain's SPF/DKIM/DMARC grade.

Just describe who you want. OpenLeads federates across the sources that fit (you don't pick one): openleads find "marketing agencies in Miami" # local businesses + their people openleads find "50 fintech founders, verified only" # YC + Hacker News openleads find "dentists in Austin" # clinics + registry records You'll see each lead stream in with a tier and a 0–100 score: safe : deliverable; sent by default. risky : kept, but held back unless you opt in. bad : dropped (no MX, disposable, unguessable). Company results are expanded into real people (founder/owner/exec) via team-page discovery. P

openleads config Interactive setup for your provider (Gmail/Workspace, Outlook/M365, Zoho, or custom), your app password (not your normal password; see your provider's docs), and your sender identity (name, org, a few lines about what you're reaching out about). Secrets are written to ~/.openleads/secrets.json ( chmod 600 ) and never leave your machine. Prefer env vars / .env ? Those still win. See sending.md .

One command does the whole pipeline (dry-run first, and always preview): openleads run "50 AI founders in SF" # preview drafts + sends openleads run "50 AI founders in SF" --live # actually send Or do it in pieces: openleads write "10 AI founders" -o drafts.json # just draft openleads send "10 AI founders" --live # find → write → send Sending honors your warmup ramp and daily cap , paces sends with human-like delays, skips anyone on your suppression list , and adds one-click unsubscribe headers. No tracking pixels, ever.

openleads web Opens http://127.0.0.1:8787 : the same engine, in your browser, fully local — a people and company database, lists, sequences, tasks, deals and analytics. See web.md . To look around first without touching your own data: openleads demo

Everything you find is saved to your workspace. Organize it, then let a sequence do the follow-up: openleads people --fit A --never-contacted # your best untouched leads openleads lists create "Q4 dentists" openleads lists add "Q4 dentists" --where dental openleads seq create "Q4 outbound" --pitch "We fill last-minute cancellations" openleads seq enroll "Q4 outbound" --list "Q4 dentists" openleads seq run "Q4 outbound" # dry run: what would send openleads seq activate "Q4 outbound" # let the scheduler run it openleads tasks --bucket today # calls and LinkedIn steps due Already have a list from

openleads stats # contacts, sends, replies, tasks, pipeline openleads inbox # optional: scan IMAP for replies & bounces openleads crm --export out.csv Replies and bounces update each contact's stage and stop their sequences automatically.

Everything is under ~/.openleads/ (override with OPENLEADS_HOME ): File What openleads.db your workspace: people, companies, lists, sequences, tasks, deals, notes, activity, plus touches, suppression and learned patterns cache.db MX / SMTP / dataset cache (speeds up re-runs) config.json non-secret preferences secrets.json API keys + mailbox credentials ( chmod 600 ) sources/*.py your own source plugins Next: Workspace · Sequences · Deliverability deep-dive · Sending guide · Web dashboard · Write a source .

The local web dashboard openleads web # → http://127.0.0.1:8787 openleads web --port 9000 # custom port openleads web --no-open # don't auto-open a browser openleads demo # the same dashboard on an invented demo workspace A full sales workspace in your browser — prospecting, a people and company database, lists, sequences, tasks, deals, templates, analytics and workflows — running on the same engine and the same local database as the CLI.

stdlib only. The server is a ThreadingHTTPServer from Python's standard library ( openleads/web/server.py ). No Flask, no Node, no build step. Bound to localhost. It listens on 127.0.0.1 , not reachable from your network. Pre-built UI. The app is plain ES modules and CSS committed under openleads/web/static/ and shipped in the wheel. End users need no toolchain . No external requests from the page. A strict same-origin Content-Security-Policy blocks third-party scripts, styles and fonts. The typeface ships inside the package, and there is no CDN and no analytics: nothing phones home.

Group Page What Workspace Home KPIs with trends (contacts, sends, reply rate, pipeline), a sends chart, the stage funnel, today's tasks, active sequences, recent activity and a setup checklist Find people Plain-English search across every free source; results stream in, already scored and saved People The contact database: filter sidebar with live counts, saved searches, configurable columns, bulk actions on a selection or every matching row, and a full contact record Companies Accounts with tech stack, size, industry and stage; profile any company from its website Lists People and company lis

Every record has its own URL, so you can bookmark or share a view on your own machine: #/people/jane@acme.com , #/companies/acme.com , #/sequences/3 , #/deals/7 , #/templates/2 . Filters live in the URL too: #/people?stage=interested&tier=safe , #/activity?show=replies .

Press ⌘K (Ctrl+K) or / anywhere to search people and companies, jump to a page, or run an action (new task, deal, sequence, template or list; import a CSV; start the task queue; find new people for what you typed). Keys Does ⌘K · / Command palette G then H, F, P, C, L, S, T, M, D, A, V, W, I Go to Home, Find, People, Companies, Lists, Sequences, Tasks, Templates, Deals, Analytics, Activity, Workflows, Import N The page's New button T Toggle dark mode ? List every shortcut Enter · S · Z In the task queue: complete, skip, snooze [ · ] On a focused deal card: move it a stage back or forward Short

Every address carries one small mark. Its shape says how OpenLeads knows the address, and its color says whether it will deliver: Mark Meaning filled square Found : published on the web or confirmed by the mail server half-filled square Pattern : built from an address format seen at that company outlined square Guessed : a common format with nothing confirming it green, amber, red Deliverable, risky, will bounce Hover a mark for the full reason; the contact record lists every check. The same marks appear in tables, records, search results and exports.

The interface follows your system theme; the moon/sun button (or T ) pins one. It uses Atkinson Hyperlegible, a typeface drawn so that characters like l , I and 1 can't be mistaken for each other, which matters when you're reading email addresses. It respects prefers-reduced-motion and works down to phone width.

The server exposes a JSON API that the UI uses and you can script against. Long-running actions stream newline-delimited JSON so progress renders live. Area Endpoints Engine GET /api/state · GET /api/sources · POST /api/find (stream) · /api/verify · /api/write · /api/send (stream) · /api/run (stream) · /api/enrich (stream) Workspace GET /api/meta · /api/home · /api/health · /api/activity People POST /api/people/search · /facets · /create · /update · /tags · /bulk · /export · GET /api/people/get Companies POST /api/companies/search · /create · /update · /bulk · /profile · /enrich (stream) · GET

The dashboard can send email from your mailbox, so it treats every other website open in your browser as hostile: Localhost only. It binds 127.0.0.1 and refuses any request whose Host header isn't a loopback name, which stops DNS-rebinding attacks. Add names with OPENLEADS_ALLOWED_HOSTS=myhost.lan if you put it behind your own proxy. No cross-site requests. Requests marked cross-site by the browser ( Sec-Fetch-Site ), or carrying an Origin other than the dashboard's own (including Origin: null from sandboxed frames and file:// pages), get 403 . JSON only. Every write must be Content-Type: appl

Finding leads: the federated engine In v4, you don't pick a data source. You describe who you want, and OpenLeads federates the query across the public sources that fit it, finds the people behind each company, verifies their email, and merges the results. This is how the big tools feel like "one box that just works", done free, keyless, and locally. openleads find "marketing agencies in Miami" openleads find "fintech founders, verified only" openleads find "dentists in Austin" openleads find "rust developers in Berlin"

The planner reads the shape of your request: Your query looks like… Federates across a place + a business category ("agencies in Miami", "law firms in London") local (OpenStreetMap) founders / startups ("fintech founders", "YC companies") yc + hn an industry / companies ("video game companies in Japan") companies (Wikidata) + edgar developers ("rust developers") github researchers ("ML researchers") openalex doctors / clinics ("dentists in Austin") npi + local a typed domain ("emails at stripe.com") domains Streams are interleaved so results stay diverse, then de-duplicated by (domain, person)

h: Time budget, output and "why so few?"
t: --budget SECONDS (default 90, 0 = no limit) is a real deadline: every network call is clamped to it, and when it runs out the search returns what already finished instead of waiting on slow sites. Late in the budget, company expansion keeps published addresses and skips team-page crawls. Transient failures (HTTP 429/5xx, timeouts) are retried briefly; OpenStreetMap queries move on to the next public Overpass mirror, then to Nominatim. openleads find "agencies in Miami" --format json | jq '.[].email' # stdout is pure JSON openleads find "agencies in Miami" -q -o leads.csv # no progress output o

Many sources return companies (a name + a domain) rather than people. OpenLeads turns those into contactable humans by reading the company's own /team , /about , and /leadership pages and extracting (name, title) pairs: JSON-LD Person objects plus conservative name/role heuristics. Each discovered person then goes through the email waterfall . Disable this with --no-people to keep company-level results (and any published role addresses).

Every source is keyless. A token (e.g. GITHUB_TOKEN ) only raises a rate limit. Source Vertical local Local businesses by category + city, via OpenStreetMap/Overpass: agencies, clinics, firms, gyms, salons, restaurants, shops. Global. yc Startup founders from the open Y Combinator dataset. hn Companies hiring now, from Hacker News "Who is hiring" (often with apply emails). companies Companies by industry + country with real websites, via Wikidata SPARQL. edgar US public companies by keyword, from SEC EDGAR. github Contactable developers via the keyless GitHub API. openalex Researchers & academ

Already have names, companies, or domains? Run the same waterfall over your list: openleads enrich my_list.csv -o enriched.csv Headers are matched forgivingly ( First Name , company , Domain , Email , …). A row with an email is verified; a row with a name + domain is resolved and verified; a row with only a domain is harvested + expanded into people. Every row comes back tiered ( safe / risky / bad ) and is saved to your local CRM.

A recipe saves an ICP + message + schedule + export and runs itself: openleads recipe add growth "marketing agencies in Miami" \ --at 09:00 --send --context "our local-SEO service" --export sheets openleads recipe run growth # dry-run now openleads schedule --at 09:00 # arm the on-device daily drip The daily drip syncs your inbox (replies/bounces stop sequences), runs due recipes, fires watchers, then sends follow-ups. A watcher delivers only new matches each run: openleads watch add new-miami "marketing agencies in Miami" --sink webhook

openleads export csv --target leads.csv openleads export sheets # a Google-Sheets-ready CSV + import hint openleads export webhook --target https://hooks.example.com/leads openleads export notion # needs notion_token + notion_database_id openleads export airtable # needs airtable_token + airtable_base openleads export hubspot # needs hubspot_token; creates/updates contacts by email csv · json · ndjson · sheets · webhook are keyless; notion , airtable and hubspot light up once you set their token in openleads config . For HubSpot, set hubspot_token in Settings → Integrations, or provide it thro

The workspace: people, companies, lists, tasks and deals Everything you find, import or add lands in one local workspace — the CRM side of OpenLeads. It's the same data in the dashboard ( openleads web ), the terminal ( openleads people , openleads tasks , …) and your AI assistant (the MCP workspace tools ). It lives in ~/.openleads/openleads.db , a SQLite file on your machine. openleads demo # try it first on an invented workspace (your data is untouched)

Every contact has the fields you'd expect from Apollo — name, title, company, email with its tier (safe / risky) and evidence (found / pattern / guessed), phone, LinkedIn, location — plus what OpenLeads works out for you: Seniority (owner, founder, C-suite, partner, VP, head, director, manager, senior, entry) and department (sales, marketing, engineering, …) from the title. Fit score , 0–100 with an A–D grade , from your ideal-customer model (see ICP scoring ). Stage , tags , lists , notes , tasks , deals , the sequence they're in, and a timeline of everything that happened. The People page is

Stage Moves here automatically when… New the contact is added Approaching the first email is sent Replied a reply arrives (with IMAP connected) Interested · Meeting booked · Customer you set it (or a deal is won → Customer) Not interested · Unresponsive you set it, or a sequence finishes with no reply (Unresponsive) Do not contact they unsubscribe, or you mark them Bad data the email bounces Automatic moves never drag a contact backwards: a follow-up sent to someone you marked Interested leaves them Interested . A reply, bounce or unsubscribe also takes the person out of any active sequence.

Companies (accounts) are created from your contacts' domains and filled in from their homepage on demand: name, description, industry, headcount band, founded year, phone, address, social profiles and the tech stack their site runs (100+ technologies across 30 categories — HubSpot, Shopify, Stripe, Intercom, WordPress, …). Filter companies by technology, industry, size, location and stage, and open one to see its people, deals, tasks and notes. openleads companies --tech HubSpot openleads companies show acme.com openleads company acme.com # live lookup of any domain, not just saved ones Accoun

Lists are static groups of people (or companies) you build from searches, selections and imports, then work as a unit: open one in the People table, put it in a sequence, export it. Tags are free-form labels on people. openleads lists create "Q4 dentists" openleads lists add "Q4 dentists" --where dental # everyone matching a search openleads lists add "Q4 dentists" jane@acme.com bob@beta.io openleads lists show "Q4 dentists"

Import & enrich → Import CSV (or openleads import ) takes an export from Apollo, HubSpot, Salesforce, LinkedIn Sales Navigator or any spreadsheet. Columns map themselves from 100+ header spellings; you can change any of them and see real values under each. Existing contacts are matched by email and updated without blanking anything . Rows with a name and a company but no email can go straight to the email finder. openleads import apollo-export.csv --preview # just show the mapping openleads import apollo-export.csv --list "Apollo import" --tags apollo \ --missing-out missing.csv openleads enri

Describe your ideal customer as points in Settings → ICP scoring : seniority, department, industry, company size, technologies, title keywords, location and reachability (verified email, phone, LinkedIn). Every contact gets a 0–100 fit score — A 75+, B 55+, C 35+, D below — and the editor previews how many grades would change and who the best matches are before you save. Each contact's record explains its score line by line.

Calls, emails, LinkedIn touches and to-dos. Sequence steps that need a human become tasks on their due date; completing one moves that contact on to their next step. The Tasks page groups work into Overdue, Today, Upcoming and No date, and Start queue works through everything due one at a time, with the contact's details, a note box, and keyboard shortcuts (Enter done, S skip, Z snooze). openleads tasks --bucket today openleads tasks add "Call Jane about pricing" --contact jane@acme.com --kind call --due tomorrow openleads tasks done 12 openleads tasks snooze 13 --due +3d

A drag-and-drop pipeline: Qualify (10%), Meeting (25%), Proposal (50%), Negotiation (75%), Won, Lost. The board shows each stage's value and probability-weighted value; the header shows open pipeline, weighted forecast, won and win rate. Winning a deal marks its contact and company as customers. openleads deals openleads deals add "Acme — annual plan" --amount 12k --contact jane@acme.com openleads deals move 3 proposal openleads deals won 3

Activity is the workspace-wide feed — sends, replies, stage changes, notes, tasks, deal moves, list and sequence changes, searches and imports — grouped by day and filterable by what happened and by record type. Data health lists what to fix before you send: unverified and guessed emails, bounces, missing titles, phones and LinkedIn, untouched contacts and unprofiled companies, each one click from the matching People filter. It also finds duplicate people (the same person at the same company under two addresses) so you can pick the record to keep and merge — tags, lists, notes, tasks, deals, s

Export any selection or filter from People as CSV, JSON, or in Apollo or HubSpot import format, or push it to Google Sheets, Notion, Airtable or a webhook. From the terminal: openleads lists export "Q4 dentists" -f hubspot -o q4.csv openleads find "…" -f apollo openleads export Settings → Data & backup (or openleads backup ) takes a consistent snapshot of the whole workspace — safe while sequences are running — into ~/.openleads/backups/ . To restore, stop OpenLeads and copy a backup over ~/.openleads/openleads.db .

Sequences A sequence is multi-step, multi-channel outreach that runs itself — the Apollo model, on your machine. Each step waits a number of days after the previous one, then either sends an email automatically or creates a task for you (a call, a LinkedIn touch, a hand-written email, any action item). People leave the sequence the moment they reply, bounce or unsubscribe. openleads seq create "Q4 outbound" --pitch "We help clinics fill last-minute cancellations" openleads seq enroll "Q4 outbound" --list "Q4 dentists" openleads seq run "Q4 outbound" # dry run: what would send right now openlea

Step What happens when it's due Automatic email Rendered for the contact and sent, inside business hours and your warmup cap Manual email A task to write and send it yourself Phone call A call task, with the contact's number one click away LinkedIn task A task with their LinkedIn profile linked Action item Any other to-do A manual step holds the contact in place until its task is completed or skipped; then they move on to the next step. New sequences start from a proven 5-step, 11-day cadence — intro email, threaded bump, call, LinkedIn, breakup — that you can edit, reorder or replace.

Email steps use template syntax , and each can have: A/B variants — every contact gets one variant (chosen deterministically from their email, so a preview matches what is sent), and the sequence page shows sends and replies per variant. Same-thread follow-ups — the step replies to the first email ( re: … ), so a bump lands in the existing conversation. AI writing — leave the variants empty and each email is written from the contact's details and the sequence's pitch, by the free LLM if you've configured one and the built-in writer otherwise. The editor's live preview renders any step for a sa

Write Get {{first_name}} the contact's first name `{{first_name\ there}}` their first name, or "there" if it's blank `{Hi\ Hey\ Hello}` one of the options, picked per contact Variables: first_name , last_name , full_name , title , company , domain , website , industry , city , country , phone , sender_name , sender_org , sender_context (the sequence's pitch, or yours from Settings) and day . Reusable emails live in Templates .

Add people from a list, a People selection (including "all N matching these filters"), the CLI, or an AI assistant over MCP. Enrollment skips — and tells you why — anyone who is: suppressed, marked do-not-contact, or bad data; not verified safe (unless the sequence allows risky emails); already in this sequence, or active in another one (unless the sequence allows overlap).

Setting Default Business hours only on automatic emails wait for your send window Skip weekends on a step due on Saturday or Sunday moves to Monday Daily limit none max automatic emails per day from this sequence, on top of your global warmup cap Allow risky emails off enroll contacts whose address isn't verified safe One sequence at a time on skip people active in another sequence Mark unresponsive on finishing with no reply moves the contact to Unresponsive Pitch your Settings pitch fills {{sender_context}} and guides AI steps

Active sequences run on the same heartbeat as everything else ( openleads schedule on , or openleads drip by hand): each tick sends the automatic emails that are due and creates the due tasks. Run now in the dashboard (or openleads seq run ) does one pass on demand — as a dry run that shows exactly what would send, or live. A dry run works on a paused sequence, so you can check one before you switch it on. Sends go through the normal sender, so the dry-run default, suppression list, warmup ramp, daily cap, business-hours window and one-click unsubscribe all apply. With IMAP connected, replies

The sequence page shows active, contacted, replied (with reply rate) and due-now counts, how many people wait at each step, sends and completed tasks per step, and replies per A/B variant. The Contacts tab lists everyone by status — active, paused, finished, replied, bounced, removed — with bulk pause, resume and remove.

Moving from Apollo OpenLeads works the way Apollo does — people and companies with filters, lists, stages, sequences, tasks and deals — so most of what you have moves straight across. Everything lands in a SQLite file on your machine.
In Apollo, open People (or a saved list), select everyone, and Export to CSV. Do the same for any other lists you want to keep as separate lists.

openleads import apollo-contacts.csv --preview # check the column mapping openleads import apollo-contacts.csv --list "From Apollo" --tags apollo or Import & enrich → Import CSV in the dashboard. Apollo's columns are recognized automatically — First Name , Last Name , Title , Company Name for Emails , Email , Person Linkedin Url , City , State , Country , # Employees , Industry , the phone columns, Website and the stage — and you can re-map any column before importing. Contacts already in OpenLeads are matched by email and updated without blanking anything . Import each Apollo list with its ow

Apollo stage OpenLeads stage Cold New Approaching Approaching Replied Replied Interested Interested Not Interested Not interested Unresponsive Unresponsive Do Not Contact Do not contact Bad Data Bad data Anything else (e.g. Changed Job ) comes in as New ; set it by hand or with openleads people stage EMAIL --to … .

Apollo's email status doesn't carry over as proof. Run the addresses through OpenLeads' own checks, which label each one found , pattern or guessed and decide safe or risky : Import & enrich → Enrich a list , or openleads enrich apollo-contacts.csv . Rows that had no email but a name and company can be found the same way ( openleads import … --missing-out missing.csv , then openleads enrich missing.csv ).

Sequences don't export from Apollo, but the shape is the same. Create one from the 5-step starter and paste your copy in: openleads seq create "Q4 outbound" --pitch "One line about what you offer" Then edit the steps in Sequences — automatic emails, manual emails, calls, LinkedIn tasks and action items, with delays, A/B variants and same-thread follow-ups. Apollo's {{first_name}} and {{company}} variables work as-is; OpenLeads also accepts fallbacks ( {{first_name|there}} ) and spintax ( {Hi|Hey} ). Reusable emails go in Templates . See the sequences guide .

Apollo's scoring doesn't move over either. Set yours in Settings → ICP scoring — seniority, department, industry, company size, technologies, title keywords and location — and preview how your contacts grade before saving. Every contact then gets a 0–100 fit score and an A–D grade you can filter and sort by.

openleads config (or Settings → Mailbox ) with an app password, then openleads doctor to check SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Turn on IMAP so replies and bounces stop sequences automatically. Sending stays inside your warmup ramp and daily cap, and everything is a dry run until you say otherwise. See sending and deliverability .

Any list or filter exports in Apollo's own import format: openleads lists export "Q4 dentists" -f apollo -o q4.csv or Export → Apollo CSV from People. HubSpot format works the same way ( -f hubspot ).

Workflows: recipes as a canvas A workflow is a recipe drawn as a row of nodes, the way n8n or Zapier draw an automation. Each node is one step of the pipeline, and clicking a node edits that step. Nothing about the engine changes: a workflow is saved as an ordinary recipe, so openleads recipe run <name> and the scheduler run it exactly the same way. openleads web # then open Workflows (under Automate) in the sidebar

Node What it does Settings Trigger When the workflow runs A schedule in plain English or cron ( weekdays 09:00 , every 2h , 0 9 * * 1-5 ), or manual only Find leads Searches the sources that fit your sentence Audience (the sentence) and how many leads Verify Scores every address and branches on the tier Safe only, or safe and risky Write Drafts a plain-text email per safe lead What you are offering, in one line Send Sends inside your warmup cap On or off, and whether to start the follow-up sequence Review Holds risky leads so nothing is sent by accident Always on Export Pushes the leads somewh

Open Workflows and click New workflow . Click Find leads and type who you want, for example marketing agencies in Miami . Click Trigger and type a schedule, or leave it on manual. Click Write and describe your offer in one line. Leave Send off for the first few runs. Turn it on once the drafts look right. Click Save .

Click Duplicate beside Delete to open an unsaved copy of the current workflow, including your latest edits and export settings. The name starts with <name>-copy ; if that name exists, it uses <name>-copy-2 , then -3 , and so on. You can edit the name and audience before saving. An untitled workflow becomes workflow-copy . The original stays unchanged, and the copy starts with no run history. Duplicating does not save or run anything. Click Save to persist the copy, or Test run to save it and start a dry run. Duplicate is unavailable while a save or test run is in progress.

Test run executes the whole workflow as a dry run. The nodes light up as each step finishes, the counts appear on each node, and the run log shows every phase. No email is sent during a test run, even with Send switched on. Scheduled runs are real runs. If Send is on, the scheduler sends inside your daily cap. Install the scheduler once with: openleads schedule on See Timed runs for how schedules are checked and what happens when your laptop was asleep.

h: Push leads into n8n or Zapier
t: Set Export to webhook and paste your n8n or Zapier webhook URL as the target. Every run POSTs the leads as newline-delimited JSON, so the rest of your automation can pick them up from there. Note: the dashboard only listens on 127.0.0.1 . A webhook export is the one place where lead data leaves your machine, and only to the URL you typed.

Deliverability: how OpenLeads decides what's safe to send The crown jewel of v3. The goal: only mark an address safe when it's genuinely likely to land , and do it without depending on outbound port 25 , which home ISPs and most clouds block. This is what separates OpenLeads from free-tier finders that quietly hand you first.last@domain guesses and let your campaign bounce.

The classic "email verifier" opens an SMTP connection to the domain's mail server and issues RCPT TO:<candidate> . If the server says 250 OK , the address exists. Two things break this: Port 25 is blocked. Residential ISPs and providers like AWS/GCP block outbound port 25 by default. The probe never connects, so the verifier either fails open (marks everything deliverable → bounces) or fails closed (marks everything undeliverable → you lose real leads). Catch-all domains. Many domains accept every address ( 250 OK for asdkfj@domain ), so a single probe tells you nothing. OpenLeads treats SMTP

All implemented in openleads/emails/ . Each is best-effort; any signal error is treated as absent, never as a false positive : the engine biases toward not marking something safe . # Signal Module Port 25? 1 MX consensus : resolved over two DoH resolvers (Google + Cloudflare); they must agree the domain has mail exchangers mx.py no 2 SPF / DMARC presence + policy, MX provider class : TXT lookups that show the domain is a real, configured mail sender mx.py no 3 Disposable / role / free-provider filtering : static lists drop info@ , noreply@ , throwaway domains, etc. patterns.py no 4 Gravatar ex

score.py is a pure function : signals → {score: 0–100, tier, confidence, reasons[]} . Because it's pure, it's exhaustively unit-tested with no network. safe : emit and send by default. Triggers include: a ground-truth exact match ; or SMTP-verified (non-catch-all); or learned-pattern match AND Gravatar hit AND healthy MX AND not catch-all ; or Gravatar hit AND common pattern AND healthy SPF/DMARC . risky : kept but not sent by default . Catch-all domains, pattern-only guesses, port-25-blocked-without-corroboration, role-ish addresses. bad : dropped. No MX, disposable, invalid syntax. confidenc

This is why OpenLeads gets more accurate the more you use it . Every ground-truth email teaches the engine that domain's convention; that lesson is stored in ~/.openleads/openleads.db ( patterns table) and applied to every future person at that domain, promoting an otherwise-unconfirmed guess to safe when corroborated. Free tiers can't do this: their database is the moat, so they have no incentive to make your guesses smarter. OpenLeads' moat is the engine , so it does.

You lose only signal #7. Signals #1–#6 still run, so you still get plenty of safe leads; they just need corroboration (ground truth, learned pattern + Gravatar, or healthy auth + common pattern) instead of a live RCPT . Run openleads doctor to see whether port 25 is open from your machine.

OpenLeads would rather under-claim than bounce your domain. A risky lead you chose to send beats a safe lead that wasn't. That conservatism is the whole point: deliverability is a reputation game, and one bad batch tanks your inbox placement. See also: Sending guide · Architecture .

Sending: cold email that lands, safely OpenLeads sends over your own mailbox, with the guardrails that separate "reaches the inbox" from "lands in spam / burns your domain." Everything here is dry-run by default ; real sends require an explicit --live (CLI) or the live toggle (web), plus a confirmation. The finder never touches your mailbox. Only run / send / campaign do.

openleads config Pick a provider preset and supply an app password (not your account password): Provider Host Port App-password docs gmail / workspace smtp.gmail.com 465 (SSL) Google App Passwords (needs 2FA) outlook / office365 smtp.office365.com 587 (STARTTLS) Microsoft App Password (Security) zoho smtp.zoho.com 465 (SSL) Zoho app-specific password custom you set smtp_host 465 or 587 your provider Credentials are stored in ~/.openleads/secrets.json ( chmod 600 ). Env vars and a local .env still take precedence (handy for CI), so nothing forces you to put secrets in the store. Verify with ope

Before a single email goes out, outreach/deliverability.py audits your sending domain and returns a readiness grade: SPF present (+30) DKIM found (+30) ← selector probe / advisory DMARC p=quarantine (+40) ───────────────────────────── grade A · 100/100 · ready SPF authorizes your provider to send for your domain. DKIM cryptographically signs your mail. DMARC tells receivers what to do with unauthenticated mail (and p=none is weak, push toward p=quarantine ). Missing pieces are the #1 reason cold email hits spam. doctor and the dashboard's Doctor page (the Deliverability badge in the sidebar) b

Brand-new mailboxes that suddenly blast 200 emails get flagged. The warmup planner ( deliverability.warmup_status ) computes today's allowance from a ramp: warmup_start = 10 # day 1 allowance warmup_step = 5 # +5 each subsequent day daily_cap = 40 # hard ceiling Day 1 → 10, day 2 → 15, … capped at daily_cap . The sender refuses to exceed the day's allowance and tells you how many remain. Tune these in openleads config (group sending ).

h: 4. How a send actually goes out
t: outreach/sender.py , for each recipient: Suppression check : skips anyone bounced / unsubscribed / replied / do-not-contact / duplicate. The suppression list is permanent and local. Warmup check : stops at the day's allowance. Human pacing : a randomized delay ( send_delay_min – send_delay_max seconds, default 25–90) between real sends. Proper headers : Message-ID , Date , threading headers, and List-Unsubscribe + List-Unsubscribe-Post (one-click). Plain-text default; no open-tracking pixels . Logged + resumable : every attempt is written to the local CRM ( touches ), so a crashed batch resume

outreach/compose.py writes each email from the lead's facts: With OPENROUTER_API_KEY set, a free LLM drafts a personalized subject + body (retried until placeholder-free). Without a key, a deterministic template is used. Either way the draft is spam-linted (spammy-word score, link count, caps ratio, length) and stripped of stray placeholders and em-dash tells. You can edit any draft before sending, in the web Compose page; your edits are exactly what's sent.

For multi-step outreach — emails with A/B variants and threaded follow-ups, plus call and LinkedIn steps that become tasks — use sequences : the dashboard's Sequences page or openleads seq . They send through this same sender, so every guardrail below applies. See the sequences guide . outreach/inbox.py (optional IMAP) detects replies and bounces; a reply stops every sequence for that person, moves them to Replied and puts a "Reply to …" task in your queue, and a bounce or unsubscribe updates suppression. Run: openleads inbox --days 21

openleads run "<query>" # find → write → send (dry-run) openleads run "<query>" --live # …for real openleads send "<query>" --live # same pipeline, terse output openleads write "<query>" -o drafts.json # stop after drafting

Dry-run everywhere; --live + confirm to send. safe -tier only unless you opt into risky . Hard daily cap + warmup ramp + human pacing. Permanent suppression; one-click unsubscribe; no tracking pixels. Per-recipient try/except, so one failure never aborts the batch. You still own compliance (CAN-SPAM, GDPR, CASL). See responsible-use.md . OpenLeads gives you the guardrails; using them well is on you.

Timed runs Save a search once and let your machine run it on a schedule: find new leads, draft emails, send them inside your daily cap, export the results, and send follow-ups. Nothing runs in the cloud.

openleads recipe add miami "marketing agencies in Miami" --every "weekdays 9am" --send openleads recipe add devs "rust developers in Berlin" --every "every 6h" --export csv --target devs.csv openleads recipe add weekly "fintech founders" -n 50 --every "mon 08:30" --every understands plain English and cron: You write It runs daily 09:00 · 9am · every day at 9:30pm once a day weekdays 8:30 · weekends 10am Mon–Fri / Sat–Sun mon,wed,fri 14:00 · tuesdays 7pm on those days hourly · every 2h · every 30m · every 90 minutes on an interval 0 9 * * 1-5 standard 5-field cron openleads recipe list shows ea

openleads schedule on # install the agent openleads schedule status # is it installed, and when does each recipe run next? openleads schedule off # remove it schedule on installs one small agent that wakes every 15 minutes and runs openleads drip --live . Each wake-up runs whatever is due, so one agent serves every schedule. It uses what your OS already has: OS Mechanism macOS a launchd agent in ~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.openleads.drip.plist Linux one crontab line, marked # OpenLeads drip heartbeat Windows a Task Scheduler task named OpenLeads Drip Change the wake-up interval with --every-min

openleads runs # the last 20 runs openleads runs -n 100 ✓ 2026-10-07T09:00:12 recipe miami 41.2s found 18 · sent 12 ✗ 2026-10-07T09:00:54 watcher new-clinics 3.1s URLError: network unreachable ✓ 2026-10-07T09:15:03 follow-ups default 0.4s due 0 · sent 0 History lives in ~/.openleads/runs.jsonl . When a run fails, the other jobs still run and you get told about it: a desktop notification on macOS and Linux, and a JSON POST to notify_webhook , if you set one. Slack, Discord, ntfy and Zapier webhooks all accept it: openleads config set notify_webhook https://hooks.slack.com/services/…

h: Run it in GitHub Actions instead
t: If you'd rather not keep a laptop awake, the OpenLeads GitHub Action runs a search on GitHub's schedule and attaches the CSV to the run: on: schedule: [{ cron: "0 13 * * 1" }] jobs: leads: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: Samyrrrrrr990/openleads@v5.1.1 id: leads with: { query: "marketing agencies in Miami", count: 50 } - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 with: { name: leads, path: "${{ steps.leads.outputs.file }}" } See examples/github-action/weekly-leads.yml . Sending from CI isn't supported; the action finds leads.

Recipes that send , and follow-ups, only go out inside the send window: weekdays, 08:00–11:00 and 13:00–16:00 local time. A sending recipe due at 7pm waits and runs at the next wake-up inside the window. Recipes that only find or export run at their exact time. openleads drip without --live is a dry run and doesn't use up a slot. Sends always respect the daily cap, warmup ramp, send-time windows and suppression list from Sending . Anyone who replies or bounces is dropped from follow-ups.

Automation & the assistant OpenLeads v3.5 can run your outreach for you: describe a campaign in one line, and let your own machine find, draft, and send it at the right time, with every message landing in your Sent folder like you typed it yourself.

h: The assistant (natural language → a configured campaign)
t: Tell OpenLeads what you want in plain English: openleads assistant "send 50 emails to fintech founders for my SaaS at 9am" It parses the audience ("fintech founders"), the count (50), what you're pitching ("my SaaS"), and the send time (9am), then finds the leads, drafts a personalized email for each, and previews everything as a dry run. Nothing is sent until you say so. You can do the same conversationally inside openleads chat : just type the request. When you ask to send or schedule , it routes to the assistant; when you ask to find , it searches. It works fully offline with a rule-based i

A campaign drafts every safe (deliverable) lead plus high-confidence risky ones, those scoring ≥ 55% on the calibrated likelihood. On the common case where outbound port 25 is blocked, a healthy authenticated corporate domain with a common pattern scores ~62%, so you still get a real, sendable batch instead of an empty list. Catch-all guesses are deliberately kept below that line.

Give a recipe a schedule and arm your machine once: openleads recipe add miami "agencies in Miami" --every "weekdays 9am" --send openleads schedule on # launchd (macOS), cron (Linux), Task Scheduler (Windows) openleads schedule status # is it installed, and what runs next? openleads runs # what ran, how long it took, what failed The agent wakes every 15 minutes and runs whatever is due: recipes, watchers and sequence follow-ups , always within your warmup/daily cap. Schedules, run history and failure alerts are covered in Timed runs . Run a cycle by hand anytime with: openleads drip # dry-run

Sends are paced like a human, not blasted: weekdays only, inside business-hour windows (08:00–11:00 and 13:00–16:00 by default), spaced apart with jitter, capped per day. Recipient time zones are inferred offline from country/city so your email lands in their morning, wherever they are.

h: Emails show up in your Sent folder
t: Mail sent over raw SMTP normally never appears in your provider's Sent folder (Gmail and Workspace are the exception: they journal it for you). OpenLeads fixes this for everyone else by saving each real send to your mailbox's IMAP Sent folder. Control it with the save_to_sent setting: Value Behavior auto (default) Save to Sent for every provider except Gmail/Workspace (which already do). always Always save (use if your Gmail setup doesn't journal sends). never Don't touch IMAP. openleads config set save_to_sent always This needs IMAP configured (it falls back to your SMTP credentials). It's be

Dry-run by default everywhere, add --live to send for real. Suppression-aware : never emails anyone who bounced, unsubscribed, or was already contacted. Warmup-capped : a fresh mailbox ramps up gradually instead of blasting day one. Plain text, a real List-Unsubscribe header, and a polite opt-out footer. See Deliverability for the sender-side reputation checks, and Sending for mailbox setup.

Use it from Claude, Cursor, or any AI tool (MCP) OpenLeads ships a Model Context Protocol server, so an AI assistant can find and verify leads for you mid-conversation: "Find 10 dentists in Austin with emails we can actually send to, and draft a short intro for each." …and work your CRM with you: "Who in my workspace is an A-grade fit and has never been contacted? Put them in a list called Q4 dentists , add them to the Local practices sequence, and make me a call task for the three most senior." It runs locally over stdio, with no extra dependencies and no keys. Searches go from your machine t

Install OpenLeads ( pip install openleads , or pipx install openleads ), then add it to your client. Claude Code claude mcp add openleads -- openleads mcp Claude Desktop ( claude_desktop_config.json ), Cursor ( ~/.cursor/mcp.json ), Windsurf , Zed and others use the same shape: { "mcpServers": { "openleads": { "command": "openleads", "args": ["mcp"] } } } No Python on the PATH? Use the npm wrapper instead: {"command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "openleads", "mcp"]} .

Tool What it does find_leads Plain-English search ("fintech founders", "law firms in London"). Returns people and companies with an email, a deliverability tier ( safe / risky ) and evidence ( found , pattern , guessed ). Takes count , verified_only , budget_seconds (default 45), optional location , source , seniority and department filters, and save_to_list to also save the results into a workspace list. find_email A name plus a company domain gives the most likely address, with evidence. verify_email Checks one address: safe , risky or bad , and why. list_sources Lists what OpenLeads can sea

Time limit. budget_seconds is a hard limit: the search returns whatever it has found by then. The default, 45 seconds, fits inside the 60-second tool-call timeout most clients use; raise it (up to 300) only if your client waits longer. Filters. location ("Austin, TX") when the place isn't in the query; source to pin one source (an unknown name comes back as an error with the closest match); seniority ( owner, founder, c_suite, partner, vp, head, director, manager, senior, entry ) and department (e.g. sales,marketing ), comma-separated. Stable shape. Every lead always has first_name , last_name

These read and change your saved workspace — the same data as the dashboard and openleads people . They never send email: enrolling someone in a sequence queues the steps, which then run on their own schedule inside your warmup cap. Tool What it does search_contacts Search saved people by text, stage, email status, seniority, department, tag, list, minimum fit score, or never contacted. get_contact One person's full record: profile, company, notes, open tasks, deals, sequences and recent activity. search_companies · get_company Companies by text, technology (e.g. HubSpot), industry or stage; o

The model sees the same honesty labels you do: found : the address was published on the web, or the mail server confirmed it. pattern : built from a pattern we saw a real address use at that domain. guessed : a common pattern with nothing confirming it. Don't send these without checking. Tell your assistant to prefer tier: safe for anything it will email.

Use it from Python Everything the CLI does is one import away. The library is standard-library only, runs locally, and shares the CLI's cache and learned email patterns (under ~/.openleads , or wherever OPENLEADS_HOME points). import openleads leads = openleads.find("dentists in Austin", count=10) for lead in leads: print(lead.email, lead.tier, lead.evidence, lead.organization) print(leads.report.summary()) # 10/10 leads in 31.4s · local ok leads.write("dentists.csv") # or .json / .jsonl import openleads stays light: the engine is only imported the first time you call find , find_email or veri

Takes the same plain-English query as openleads find and returns a SearchResult — a list of Lead objects that also carries the parsed query and the run report. Option Default Meaning count None How many leads to return (1–1000). Default: the number in the query ("50 fintech founders"), else 10. location None A place, if it isn't in the words ( "Austin, TX" ). source None Pin one source (see openleads sources ). By default the query is routed to the sources that fit it. verified_only False Keep only safe -tier (deliverable) addresses. budget 60 Seconds before the search returns what it has. 0 =

It is a list : index it, loop over it, len() it. .query — the Query that ran (the parsed words plus your options). .report — what happened, per source (see below). .to_dicts() / .to_json() — the same shape as openleads find --format json . .write(path, fmt=None) — csv , json or jsonl ( ndjson ), picked from the file extension unless you pass fmt . Returns the path.

The fields of the CSV export, as attributes: first_name , last_name , email , title , organization , industry , employees , linkedin_url , city , country , website , phone , seniority , department , company_size , technologies , socials , description , source , vertical — plus tier — safe (send), risky (plausible, unconfirmed) or bad ; confidence_pct — a calibrated 0–100 deliverability likelihood; evidence — found (published or confirmed by the mail server), pattern (built from an address shape seen at that domain), guessed , or none ; reasons — a short human explanation of the tier; contact_t

leads.report is a SearchReport : rep = leads.report rep.summary() # "4/10 leads in 60.8s · time budget reached · local ok · yc timeout" rep.status_lines() # one line per source rep.hints() # what to try next when a search came up short rep.stop_reason # count_reached | exhausted | budget | futility | max_companies rep.dropped # {"undeliverable": 3, "not_safe": 0, "filtered": 2} rep.sources["local"] # SourceReport: status, entities, expanded, leads, seconds, # fallbacks, errors, note, reason rep.to_dict() # JSON-ready A source's status is one of: Status Meaning ok Returned results without troub

r = openleads.find_email("Ada Lovelace", "acme.com") r.email, r.tier, r.confidence_pct, r.reasons Returns an EmailResult with the most likely address and its evidence. Options: deep=False , use_cache=True .
openleads.verify("ada@acme.com").tier # "safe" | "risky" | "bad" A failed DNS lookup is reported as risky ("couldn't check the mail server"), never as "no mail server".

openleads.engine.build_leads(query, cache=None, db=None, on_progress=None, *, report=None) is what find wraps. Build the Query with openleads.intent.build_query(text, **options) — the same validated builder the CLI, the dashboard and the MCP server use. on_progress(kind, payload) receives "phase" (a message), "lead" (a Lead ), "scan" (counts), "source" (a SourceReport , when a source finishes) and "report" (the SearchReport , at the end); ignore kinds you don't use.

Variable Effect OPENLEADS_HOME Where the cache and database live (default ~/.openleads ). OPENLEADS_HTTP_RETRIES Retries per request on HTTP 429/502/503/504, timeouts and dropped connections (default 2 , max 5 ). OPENLEADS_OVERPASS_URLS Comma-separated Overpass endpoints to use instead of the public mirrors. OPENLEADS_CONTACT An email or URL added to the User-Agent sent to public APIs (Nominatim, Overpass, Wikidata, SEC…), as their usage policies ask for heavy use. GITHUB_TOKEN Higher GitHub API limits for developer searches.

Writing a source plugin A source is the only thing standing between OpenLeads and a new vertical. Everything downstream (email finding, SMTP verification, scoring, caching, CSV/JSON/NDJSON output, the chat CLI) is already done. You just teach OpenLeads how to discover people from some free, public dataset. This is the highest-leverage contribution you can make: one small file turns OpenLeads into "Apollo for <your vertical> ".

A source is a subclass of openleads.sources.base.Source that yields normalized Entity records: from typing import Iterator from openleads.sources.base import Source from openleads.models import Entity, Query class Source: name: str # registry key, lowercase, e.g. "lawyers" kind: str # "company" | "people" vertical: str # human label, e.g. "attorneys" description: str # one line shown by `openleads sources` def search(self, query: Query) -> Iterator[Entity]: ...

Entity( full_name="Ada Lovelace", # required for person email-finding title="Partner", organization="Acme LLP", domain="acme.law", # email domain if known/derivable ("" = none) website="https://acme.law", location="San Francisco, USA", links={"linkedin": "...", "bar_id": "..."}, # any profile URLs/ids extra={"industry": "Law", "city": "SF", "country": "USA", "vertical": "attorneys"}, # surfaced in output source=self.name, ) If you set domain , the engine finds and verifies an email automatically. If you don't (many public registries have no email/website), the engine still emits the record, si

Query carries what the user asked for. Use what's relevant to your dataset: field meaning count how many leads the user wants (cap your fetch around this) keyword / industry free-text topic/specialty (e.g. "fintech", "pediatric") location place filter title role filter verified_only the engine applies this for you; you can ignore it max_companies scan budget (for sources that page through many entities)

Drop a *.py file into ~/.openleads/sources/ . It's auto-discovered on the next run. Great for private/company-specific sources you don't want to publish. # ~/.openleads/sources/crm_export.py import csv from openleads.sources.base import Source from openleads.models import Entity, Query class CRMExportSource(Source): name = "crm" kind = "people" vertical = "my CRM export" description = "Reads contacts from ~/contacts.csv and verifies their emails." def search(self, query: Query): with open("/Users/me/contacts.csv", newline="") as f: for i, row in enumerate(csv.DictReader(f)): if i >= query.coun

h: 2. A built-in source: contribute it back
t: Add a module under openleads/sources/ (e.g. lawyers.py ), implement the class, add a fixture-based parse test under tests/ , and open a PR. The registry finds any Source subclass defined in the package automatically.

Use the shared helpers so you get caching and a sane User-Agent for free: from openleads._http import get_json, get_text def search(self, query): data = get_json("https://api.example.com/people?q=...", cache=self.cache, ttl_ns="dataset") # cached ~1 day ... self.cache is injected by the engine before search() runs (may be None when caching is disabled). Pass it straight through to get_json / get_text . Be polite: prefer keyless public APIs, respect rate limits, add small delays when paging, and degrade gracefully (return fewer/no results, never crash) when a service is down or its shape change

Keep the network-touching part thin and the parsing pure, then test the parser with a saved fixture (no network): def test_my_source_parse(): sample = {"results": [{"name": "Ada", "firm": "Acme", "domain": "acme.law"}]} ents = MySource()._parse(sample) # a pure helper you wrote assert ents[0].domain == "acme.law" That's it. Ship a vertical in ~30 lines.

Architecture OpenLeads is a small, readable Python package built around one idea: a universal deliverability engine fed by pluggable sources, that also writes and sends — with a local sales workspace (people, companies, lists, sequences, tasks, deals) on top. The core library is 100% standard library (zero runtime dependencies), the verify engine, the SMTP sender, and the web server are all stdlib. The pretty chat TUI and the LLM-drafting convenience live behind optional extras. openleads/ ├── cli.py argparse front-end: find · run · write · send · sources · verify · │ inbox · crm · config · do

sequenceDiagram participant U as User (chat / CLI) participant I as intent.py participant E as engine.py participant S as Source plugin participant M as emails/ (MX+SMTP) participant K as cache (sqlite) U->>I: "50 fintech founders verified" I-->>E: Query(source=yc, count=50, ...) E->>S: search(query) loop per entity (until count) S-->>E: Entity(name, domain, ...) E->>M: find_email(name, domain) M->>K: MX cached? K-->>M: hit / miss → DoH lookup (Google + Cloudflare) M->>M: SMTP RCPT probe (+ catch-all) M-->>E: EmailResult(email, label, score 0–100) end E-->>U: stream leads → CSV / JSON / NDJSON

All state lives in one SQLite file, ~/.openleads/openleads.db , opened in WAL mode with a busy timeout so the dashboard, the scheduler and the CLI can share it. Schema changes are versioned migrations in schema.py , tracked with PRAGMA user_version and applied in a single BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction, so an old database upgrades itself the first time a new version opens it. Table Holds leads one row per person: structured columns (name, title, company, phone, LinkedIn, location, seniority, department, stage, owner, fit score, …) plus the original record as JSON accounts one row per company doma

Zero dependencies in the core. Engine + library are stdlib only, easy to audit, trivial to run. Pretty TUI and sending are opt-in extras. One job per unit. Sources discover; the email engine verifies; writers format; the cache remembers. Each is testable in isolation, mostly without the network. Inverted moat. Coverage scales by adding sources, not by owning a database. The email engine is vertical-agnostic. Honest confidence. Guesses are labeled as guesses and scored 0–100; domain-less records (e.g. NPI) are surfaced without faking emails. Polite by default. Connection reuse, small delays, mu
How the email engine works The part of OpenLeads people care about most is how it finds and verifies an email for free . Here's the whole thing, no magic.

h: 1. From a name + domain to candidates
t: Given Ada Lovelace at acme.io , OpenLeads generates the email patterns that real companies actually use, in rough order of likelihood: first.last@ ada.lovelace@acme.io firstlast@ adalovelace@acme.io first@ ada@acme.io flast@ alovelace@acme.io first_last@ ada_lovelace@acme.io f.last@ a.lovelace@acme.io last@ lovelace@acme.io

h: 2. Does the domain even accept mail? (MX lookup, cross-checked)
t: Before bothering a mail server, OpenLeads asks for the domain's MX (mail exchanger) records over DNS-over-HTTPS , and it asks two independent resolvers (Google and Cloudflare): GET https://dns.google/resolve?name=acme.io&type=MX GET https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?name=acme.io&type=MX -> aspmx.l.example.com, alt1.aspmx.l.example.com, ... Querying two resolvers does two things: it survives one provider being down , and it lets OpenLeads reward agreement : when both resolvers return the same mail exchangers, that's a stronger signal than one. No MX records at all → the domain can't receive

This is the core trick. Email delivery is a short conversation. OpenLeads has the beginning of that conversation and then hangs up before any message is sent: S: 220 aspmx.l.google.com ESMTP C: HELO openleads.local S: 250 Hello C: MAIL FROM:<verify@yourdomain.com> S: 250 OK C: RCPT TO:<ada@acme.io> S: 250 OK <-- mailbox exists ✅ C: QUIT A 250 / 251 on RCPT TO means the server will accept mail for that address, i.e. the mailbox exists. A 550 means it doesn't. No DATA command is ever sent, so no email is delivered. This is exactly what paid verifiers do; it's just SMTP.

Some domains accept every address ( anything@domain.com returns 250 ), which makes per-mailbox verification meaningless. OpenLeads detects this by first probing a random, impossible address: C: RCPT TO:<qk7zx9plmn4w@acme.io> S: 250 OK <-- accepts garbage = catch-all If the random probe is accepted, the domain is flagged catch-all and the best-pattern guess is labeled catch_all_guess instead of verified . Honesty over vanity numbers.

Every result keeps a human label and an explainable numeric score, so you can sort and threshold programmatically. Label Meaning verified A specific mailbox returned 250 and the domain is not catch-all. High confidence. catch_all_guess Domain accepts everything; we return the most likely pattern but can't prove it. pattern_guess Domain has MX but SMTP verification wasn't possible (e.g. port 25 blocked, greylisting). Best-effort. none No MX (unusable domain), or a domain-less public record (e.g. an NPI doctor with no email). The score (0–100) is built from independent signals, each adding or su

OpenLeads keeps a small SQLite cache at ~/.openleads/cache.db : What TTL MX lookups (per domain) 7 days SMTP verification (per name+domain) 14 days Source datasets (e.g. the YC dump) 1 day A cache hit short-circuits the network entirely, so re-runs are near-instant and mail servers aren't probed twice for the same thing. Manage it with openleads cache info / openleads cache clear , or bypass it with --no-cache .

Port 25 must be reachable outbound. Many cloud hosts allow it; some residential ISPs block it. When blocked, OpenLeads falls back to pattern guesses. Big providers (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365) sometimes greylist or accept-all, reducing how many you can hard-verify. That's expected. OpenLeads paces its probes (small delays, reuses one connection per domain) to be a polite network citizen. Please don't remove those delays.
Responsible use OpenLeads is a powerful, free tool. With that comes responsibility. Read this before running campaigns.
Legitimate B2B outreach (sales, partnerships, sponsorships) Recruiting and talent sourcing Research on startup ecosystems Building your own CRM/prospecting workflows

Spam, bulk unsolicited blasting, or buying/selling scraped lists Harassment, scams, phishing, or any deceptive messaging Scraping behind logins or violating a site's Terms of Service Circumventing rate limits or hammering mail servers

Cold email is legal in many places if you follow the rules . You are responsible for compliance, which may include: CAN-SPAM (US): truthful headers/subject, a valid physical address, a working unsubscribe, and honoring opt-outs promptly. GDPR / ePrivacy (EU/UK): have a lawful basis (often "legitimate interest" for B2B), honor objections, and disclose how you got the contact. CASL (Canada): stricter consent rules, understand them before emailing Canadians. This is not legal advice. When in doubt, consult a professional.

h: Be a good citizen of the network
t: Keep the built-in rate limits and delays . They protect mail servers and your sending reputation. Verification probes never send mail, but they still touch other people's infrastructure, don't run them at abusive volume. Use a dedicated sending domain/mailbox , warm it up, and watch your bounce rate. High bounces hurt deliverability for everyone on your domain. Send relevant, personalized, low-volume outreach. It performs better anyway.
